subtype: Approach: tracking where time actually goes for a week [Thinking]
passage: For a week I kept a tally on a sticky note stuck to my monitor. Every time I answered a work message after six, I made a tick; every late meeting, a dash; every real emergency, a star. I had been feeling guilty all month, sure I was always behind. By Friday the note told a different story: forty-one ticks, six dashes, one star. Nearly all my late hours were replies to chat pings that could have waited. The one star was a failing build that Pema and I fixed together. Seeing the numbers, the vague guilt shrank into something I could work with. I can decide about pings. I cannot decide about a broken build. - Gargi

qa.q: How many real emergencies did Gargi count in the week?
qa.a: Gargi counted one, the failing build.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel about work before keeping the tally?
qa.a: Gargi felt guilty and sure of always being behind.

qa.q: What could Gargi try next, based on the tally?
qa.a: Gargi could check chats at set times in the evening instead of answering each ping, and agree with colleagues how to flag a real emergency.

qa.q: How might Pema see the tally?
qa.a: Pema, who helped fix the build, may see the emergency as real but rare, and may welcome clearer signals about what is urgent.

grounding: Gargi logs a week of late messages, meetings and emergencies, and finds most late work was replying to chats.
